extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students or readers learning basic mathematical logic and proof techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Introductory chapter-level guidance on propositional logic and basic proof techniques: definitions (statement, open sentence), logical connectives, truth tables, implication and proof patterns (modus ponens/tollens, contrapositive, chaining), and common fallacies and notational/style advice for writing clear mathematical arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement (declarative sentence with definite truth value)
rubrics_metrics.description: A declarative sentence that can be assigned a definite truth value (true or false) is called a statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The number √2 is not a rational number.' is a statement (true); 'The number 17 is even.' is a statement (false). Avoid ambiguous sentences where the truth value cannot be decided (e.g., 'I am tall' without identifying the speaker).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open sentence (depends on variables/domain)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences whose truth value depends on the value(s) of variable(s) are open sentences (not statements until variables are instantiated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'x^2 − 5x + 4 = 0' is an open sentence; over integers it is true for x=1,4 and false otherwise. Always clarify the domain for variables (integers, reals, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid self-referential sentences and paradoxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-referential sentences that assert their own falsity or refer circularly are not suitable starting points; they create paradoxes and are difficult to work with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and pointers: 'This sentence is false' and Russell's paradox (set R = {X | X ∉ X}). The text advises avoiding such constructions at this stage and refers interested readers to foundational literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation for statements and open sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Use single-letter uppercase names (P, Q, R) for statements and P(x), Q(x) for open sentences depending on variable(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mirrors function-like notation: provide values for variables to obtain statements (e.g., P(1) true, P(2) false). When open sentences depend on multiple variables, use commas: P(x,k).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation definition and notation consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Negation of a statement P, denoted ∼P (also written !P or ¬P), is true exactly when P is false and false exactly when P is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise all three notations but pick one and stick with it for clarity. Examples: negation of 'It is Tuesday' is 'It is not Tuesday'; double-negation ∼(∼P) has same truth values as P.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth tables as a primary verification tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth tables make truth values precise for statements and compound statements and help reduce complicated combinations to mechanical verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use truth tables to compare connectives, verify tautologies, and understand compound statements. The chapter shows tables for negation, conjunction, disjunction, implication, contrapositive, converse, inverse, and biconditional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjunction and disjunction definitions (and/or)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjunction P ∧ Q is true iff both P and Q are true. Disjunction P ∨ Q is true if at least one of P or Q is true (inclusive or).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that colloquial 'or' can be exclusive; in mathematical contexts assume inclusive or unless 'but not both' is explicitly stated. Use words to clarify when exclusivity is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish logical connectives from set notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not confuse ∨/∧ (logical or/and) with ∪/∩ (set union/intersection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful with symbols and their semantic domains; the book explicitly warns against interchanging them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implication (conditional) truth definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The implication 'If P then Q' (P ⇒ Q) is false exactly when P is true and Q is false; otherwise it is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer reading/writing 'If P then Q' to keep hypothesis before conclusion. The text notes many alternative phrasings exist but recommends avoiding those that reverse order (e.g., 'Q if P') until more experience is gained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation and usage of necessary vs sufficient conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: P is sufficient for Q means P ⇒ Q; Q is necessary for P means P ⇒ Q (emphasis differs depending on context).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these terms to emphasize hypothesis or conclusion as needed. The text gives examples of phrasing and advises care with emphasis and reader comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof strategy for implications (assume hypothesis true)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove an implication P ⇒ Q holds for all relevant domain elements, assume P is true and prove Q; you do not need to consider the case P is false (implication is then automatically true).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because an implication is only false when P true and Q false, proofs conventionally begin by assuming P and deriving Q; the text notes authors often leave 'P false' unstated because readers know the truth-table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modus ponens (valid deduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: From P ⇒ Q and P, deduce Q (this valid deduction is called modus ponens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use modus ponens when you have an established implication and the hypothesis holds; historically noted as formalised by Theophrastus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modus tollens (valid deduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: From P ⇒ Q and ¬Q, deduce ¬P (this valid deduction is called modus tollens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when you know the implication and can show the conclusion is false to infer hypothesis false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid common fallacies: affirming the consequent
rubrics_metrics.description: The invalid deduction 'P ⇒ Q; Q; therefore P' is fallacious (affirming the consequent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show how this leads to nonsense (e.g., if 'If they are Galileo then they are suppressed' and 'I am suppressed' cannot justify 'I am Galileo'). The chapter flags this as a frequent error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid common fallacies: denying the antecedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The invalid deduction 'P ⇒ Q; ¬P; therefore ¬Q' is fallacious (denying the antecedent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate why this is wrong (e.g., not having been to Toronto doesn't imply not having visited Canada).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chaining/transitivity of implications
rubrics_metrics.description: If P ⇒ R and R ⇒ Q, then P ⇒ Q (implication composition / transitivity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proving P ⇒ Q, break it into smaller implications P ⇒ P1 ⇒ P2 ⇒ ... ⇒ Q; use chaining and repeated modus ponens to conclude Q when P holds. The book demonstrates via truth-table and reasoning that the composed implication is a tautology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrapositive when helpful
rubrics_metrics.description: The contrapositive (¬Q ⇒ ¬P) has the same truth table as P ⇒ Q and can be easier to prove in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text suggests proving the contrapositive instead of the original implication if it simplifies reasoning (example: proving 'If n^2 is odd then n is odd' via its contrapositive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Converse and inverse are not equivalent to original implication
rubrics_metrics.description: The converse Q ⇒ P and the inverse ¬P ⇒ ¬Q do not generally have the same truth table as P ⇒ Q (though converse and inverse share a table).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter warns against assuming converse/inverse hold and recommends checking them separately; provides examples (Shakespeare/dead).

rubrics_metrics.name: Biconditional (iff) definition and equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: The biconditional P ⇐⇒ Q ('P if and only if Q') is true exactly when P and Q have the same truth value; equivalently P ⇐⇒ Q ≡ (P ⇒ Q) ∧ (Q ⇒ P).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'iff' to state necessary and sufficient conditions. The text notes common alternative abbreviations ('iff', 'is equivalent to').

rubrics_metrics.name: Make definitions and counting conventions explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions (even seemingly minor ones like indexing decimal digits) affect truth values; state conventions explicitly when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: whether the 100th decimal digit of π is 7 depends on whether you count the leading '3' as the first decimal digit. The book emphasizes that 'definitions matter.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer clear phrasing and explicit clarification over terse/ambiguous notation
rubrics_metrics.description: When notation or ordinary language could be ambiguous (e.g., exclusive/inclusive or, 'Q if P' ordering), prefer using more words to avoid reader confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice repeated: if in doubt, clarify with words rather than saving symbols at the expense of clarity. The author recommends avoiding phrasings that put conclusion before hypothesis until more experienced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical connectives are sufficient to construct any two-statement truth table
rubrics_metrics.description: Using 'not', 'and', and 'or' one can construct any truth table of two statements (there are 2^4 = 16 possibilities); familiar derived operators include NAND, NOR, XOR, XNOR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text references computer-science operators and indicates these can be built from the basic three connectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples and thought experiments to test understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrative examples (e.g., exam passing, Shakespeare examples, parity facts) help build intuition about truth tables and implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work through the four rows of the implication truth-table with concrete scenarios to see when an implication is false vs true; use such examples when teaching or writing proofs to anticipate reader confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise practice to consolidate logical skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Active exercises (classifying statements, writing symbolic forms, constructing truth tables, applying deductions) are essential for mastering the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter provides numerous exercises asking to distinguish statements vs open sentences, convert between symbolic and English forms, and use truth tables to verify equivalences or deduce conclusions from implications.
